item.title: Mamata, Kejriwal and Dipke among hundreds detained, Delhi locked down to foil protest
item.description:
INDIA-POLITICS/GEN Z

Police detained hundreds of protesters and the "Cockroach" youth movement founder in Delhi on Saturday as security forces locked down parts of the capital to thwart a demonstration demanding the resignation of India's election chief.

Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the city, mobile internet services were suspended in the central business district and dozens of metro stations and markets were shut as authorities moved to stop a rally organised by the Cockroach movement.

The protest was aimed at Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The movement had planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in central Delhi. But the area was sealed off by security forces before the demonstration began.

However, small protests broke out elsewhere in the city, including at a popular crafts market and the memorial to freedom movement leader Mahatma Gandhi, with protesters shouting slogans demanding Kumar's resignation.

"Long live the revolution," some young protesters chanted in central Delhi as police chased them and dragged scores of others into buses to be taken away, even as more arrived, a Reuters witness said.

"This is violating the rights of the people and the country will not tolerate this anymore," Yogendra Solanki told Reuters as police escorted him away.

Police also detained Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and senior leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka when their flight from Mumbai landed in Delhi, the group said in a statement.

Delhi locked down to foil protest

Television footage showed Dipke challenging officers who approached him on board the aircraft.

"I have come to be arrested, arrest me ... I am not afraid of you guys," he said.

"No, this is not an arrest," one officer replied. "Please cooperate."

The movement condemned what it called the "authoritarian detention" of its leaders, demanded their immediate release and said the protest would continue regardless.

Some opposition lawmakers and former chief ministers Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal and Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi were also detained, TV channels showed.

Representatives of two digital news outlets said police briefly detained four of their reporters while they were covering the demonstrations. A Reuters journalist was also detained briefly before being released.

Some lawyers protesting outside the Supreme Court were also picked up and later freed, according to the president of the court's bar association.
There was no immediate comment from police on the detentions.

Across the sprawling capital of about 20 million people, security forces mounted checkpoints on major roads and at city entry points. Police officers boarded buses searching for protesters, while vehicles were subjected to inspections.

Barricades and concrete blocks stopped traffic, while anti-riot vehicles mounted with tear gas guns were stationed on key routes.

New challange to Modi

The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi, stemming from allegations that election authorities improperly revised voter rolls ahead of recent state polls.

Protests have gathered momentum since last week, when the Indian Express newspaper reported that two election commissioners had questioned and disagreed with Kumar over revisions that removed roughly 130 million names from voter lists.

Kumar has not commented but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied allegations of wrongdoing.

The BJP says its electoral success reflects Modi's popularity and India's economic growth, and accuses opposition parties of spreading misinformation because they have failed to win elections.

Nonetheless, the near daily protests pose a new challenge for Modi, just months after demonstrations over exam paper leaks forced his education minister to quit.

The unrest also comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027.

Saturday's restrictions showed Modi's government had "officially waged war against its own people", KC Venugopal, a senior leader of the main opposition Congress party said.

BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra said democracy had prevailed over mob rule.

Deletions affected state polls, opposition alleges

Opposition parties say the voter deletions affected the outcome of some recent state elections won by the BJP, and have cast a shadow on elections in the world's largest democracy.

Election Commission data show about 130 million voter entries were removed during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated, 30 million who could not be traced and 28 million who had died.

The commission says the removals relate to entries identified during the draft revision process and that any eligible voter incorrectly deleted can re-enrol.

item.title: Mamata Banerjee detained in Delhi
item.description:
Former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee was detained by Delhi Police on Saturday after staging a sit-in on a road near the South Avenue bus stand in New Delhi, amid escalating protests demanding the removal of India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
According to live updates reported by Hindustan Times, Banerjee was taken into custody while holding a dharna against the election chief.
The Trinamool Congress leader had earlier indicated that she might join a demonstration organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) at Jantar Mantar, where protesters were demanding Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls.
Her reported detention came amid a sweeping security operation across the Indian capital, with police detaining more than 1,000 people ahead of Saturday’s demonstration.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and two other senior leaders were also detained after arriving at Delhi airport, according to Hindustan Times.
Authorities deployed thousands of security personnel, barricaded major roads, restricted mobile internet access and disrupted metro services to prevent protesters from gathering in central Delhi.
The protests centre on allegations that the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls has resulted in the wrongful removal of millions of eligible voters.
The Election Commission has rejected allegations of deliberate manipulation, maintaining that the exercise is intended to identify duplicate and ineligible entries.
Delhi Police said permission for the Jantar Mantar demonstration had been denied because organisers submitted their application too late and cited public-order concerns.
The confrontation has intensified political tensions between Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and opposition parties over the independence and functioning of India’s election authorities.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,155 as eight die in 24 hours
item.description:
Eight more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Saturday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,155.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all eight of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,051, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 104, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the eight new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in Dhaka, with five deaths reported in both the Dhaka division and Dhaka district.
A total of 955 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Saturday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 203,848.
During the same period, 131 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 22,328.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 180,945 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 173,454 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: YouTuber Dhruv Rathee detained by Delhi Police; CJP demands release
item.description:
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee was detained by Delhi Police at his residence in Gurugram’s Sector 56 on Saturday ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) planned protest at Jantar Mantar, NDTV reported, citing police sources.
Rathee had arrived to join the demonstration, prompting heightened security arrangements across the national capital.
According to sources, around 50 Delhi Police personnel arrived at Rathee’s Gurugram residence on Saturday morning and detained him.
The detention drew a sharp response from the CJP, which demanded his “immediate release”.
On Friday evening, Rathee announced his participation in Saturday’s protest in a video posted on his X account.
A vocal critic of the Narendra Modi government, Rathee arrived in India from Germany earlier this week and joined a CJP protest in Bengaluru on October 8.
Rathee has a substantial online following, with 19.2 million Instagram followers, 3.3 million on X, and 33 million YouTube subscribers.
Earlier this week, Delhi Police denied permission for the protest, citing security concerns and procedural requirements.
Police have stepped up preventive detentions and deployed personnel at strategic locations to prevent protesters from reaching the protest site.
More than 400 people were detained overnight, while hundreds of trains were cancelled and dozens of metro stations shut ahead of a large-scale protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in central Delhi on Saturday.
The CJP mobilised supporters to gather at Jantar Mantar, while the Centre deployed more than 20,000 police and Central Armed Police Forces personnel to maintain law and order.

item.title: Tagore mural targeted outside Shilpakala Academy, one detained
item.description:
Police detained ANM Ayas, a leader of Rashtra Sanglap Forum, on Saturday afternoon for allegedly attempting to deface a mural of Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore outside Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy in the capital’s Segunbagicha area.
The incident occurred just five days after Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) cleared the footpath of encroachments and decorated an adjoining wall with portraits of 10 prominent figures from Bengali literature, art and culture.
Shahbag Police Station Sub-Inspector Abdul Khalek confirmed the detention, saying Ayas had been taken to the police station after attempting to erase Tagore’s portrait.
The incident comes amid criticism over the selection of cultural personalities featured in the murals, particularly the inclusion of figures from West Bengal and the absence of women.
According to reports, police intervened after an attempt was made to apply black or white paint to the portraits outside the academy.
The Daily Campus reported that three people, including Ayas, were detained in connection with the incident. Other reports initially confirmed only Ayas’s detention.
The Daily Campus also described Ayas as president of Rashtra Sanglap Forum, while other outlets identified him as its member secretary.
On October 5, DSCC reopened the Segunbagicha footpath following an operation to remove encroachments.
As part of the renovation, portraits of 10 cultural figures were painted on a roadside wall near Shilpakala Academy.
They included Rabindranath Tagore, national poet Kazi Nazrul Islam, Shilpacharya Zainul Abedin, filmmaker Satyajit Ray, philosopher and social reformer Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Fakir Lalon Shah, artist SM Sultan, filmmaker Zahir Raihan, folk singer Shah Abdul Karim and actor Humayun Faridi.
The project also included new dustbins, benches for pedestrians and repairs to the boundary wall.
The newly renovated stretch was opened to pedestrians after the removal of makeshift shops and other obstructions.
It was not immediately clear whether any formal case had been filed or what further legal action police intended to take.

item.title: CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, two others detained aboard plane in Delhi
item.description:
Police detained Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder Abhijit Dipke and two other party members aboard an aircraft shortly after it landed at Delhi Airport, ahead of the party’s planned protest at Jantar Mantar, reports NDTV.
Dipke went live on Instagram as police entered the aircraft. The video shows officers detaining Dipke, Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka inside the plane.
The footage captures a commotion as CJP members questioned the police over their decision to detain them before passengers had disembarked.
In the video, Dipke is heard telling female police officers: “You could have waited for us to step out. Come, arrest us. We are not afraid.”

item.title: States told by Indian govt to stop protest march to Delhi
item.description:
India’s Union Ministry of Home Affairs has asked all states and Union Territories to coordinate with Delhi Police and take preventive measures to stop protesters from travelling to the national capital ahead of a planned demonstration by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), The Hindu reported.
In a letter to state chief secretaries and police chiefs on Friday, Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan flagged the “grave law and order and public order implications” of the planned protest at Jantar Mantar on Saturday.
The protesters are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over concerns about the Election Commission’s functioning and its handling of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
Authorities have introduced sweeping restrictions ahead of the demonstration. These include preventive detentions, train cancellations, the closure of metro stations and the suspension of mobile internet services in parts of central Delhi.
The restrictions have drawn criticism from protest organisers, who have described the measures as intimidation by the authorities.
In its letter, the Union government said Delhi Police had rejected the organisers’ request to hold the demonstration at Jantar Mantar, ANI reported.
The ministry also cited what it described as a “documented history of non-compliance with lawful directions” by the CJP and organisations supporting it during an earlier protest. It alleged that the previous demonstration, involving participants from several states, had disrupted public order and damaged public property, The Hindu reported.
The ministry said intelligence inputs suggested that CJP members and supporters planned to defy prohibitory orders and enter Delhi through multiple routes.
It directed states and Union Territories to “immediately operationalise preventive measures” in coordination with Delhi Police to maintain public order and protect critical infrastructure.
The government also stressed the need for real-time intelligence sharing among state agencies, transit authorities and Delhi Police to ensure coordinated action.
The planned demonstration follows several days of protests by opposition INDIA bloc members in Delhi and other parts of India, calling for Kumar’s resignation over concerns about electoral roll revisions and the functioning of the Election Commission.

item.title: Mahatma Gandhi’s great-grandson detained in Mumbai ahead of CJP protest
item.description:
Mumbai Police detained Tushar Gandhi, great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi and president of Hum Bharat Ke Log, along with his associates on Saturday as they headed to August Kranti Maidan for a protest in support of the Cockroach Janata Party’s (CJP) demonstration in Delhi, The Indian Express reported.
The protest was scheduled for 3:30pm.
A police official said Gandhi was picked up from Bandra and taken to DN Nagar police station. Gandhi claimed on X that he had been arrested and taken to an unknown location. Police denied arresting him, saying he had only been detained.
Guddi S L, vice-president of the organisation, was picked up from Andheri and taken to MIDC police station, police confirmed.
On Friday, Gandhi posted a poster on X urging Mumbaikars to join him at August Kranti Maidan, the site from which the Quit India movement was launched in 1942. The protest was planned in support of the CJP’s demand for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Gamdevi Police said no application had been received or permission granted for the demonstration.
“Due to a Supreme Court ruling, the Mumbai police cannot grant permission to hold a protest at August Kranti Maidan as the land belongs to the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI). No one had approached us in the first instance,” a senior police official said on Friday.
Guddi disputed the claim, saying she had emailed police seeking permission because Gandhi was not in the city but had received no response.
“Gandhi has been called by the police, and they are telling him not to protest. They have also asked him about his location and said that they would detain him,” she said on Friday.
The detentions come amid heightened police vigilance across Maharashtra ahead of the CJP’s planned protest at Jantar Mantar. Police in Mumbai and other parts of the state have been monitoring people suspected of planning to travel to Delhi.
Mumbai Police detained more than 200 people on Friday to prevent them from travelling to the national capital, the report said.

item.title: Two crude bombs hurled outside PM’s Office, police seek suspects
item.description:
Two crude bombs, were hurled outside the Prime Minister’s Office in Tejgaon, Dhaka, early Saturday, prompting police to launch an investigation to identify and arrest those involved.
The incident occurred around 1:15am. One of the bombs exploded, while the other was safely detonated in a controlled explosion by the Bomb Disposal Unit of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s (DMP) Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crime (CTTC) unit.
DMP Tejgaon Division Deputy Commissioner Ibne Mizan said police were working to identify and arrest the two suspects who arrived on a motorcycle.
According to him, the two men reached the area around 1:15am, surveyed their surroundings for two to three minutes, hurled the bombs and fled. Police received information that they headed towards Kafrul via Agargaon.
Ibne Mizan said police teams began investigating immediately after the incident. Footage from nearby CCTV cameras has been collected to help identify the suspects, and the incident is being treated as a priority.

item.title: Job seekers block roads in Dhaka over youth development exam paper leak
item.description:
Job seekers blocked several major roads in Dhaka on Saturday to protest the alleged leak of question papers for the Department of Youth Development’s recruitment examination, disrupting traffic in several areas.
Around noon, protesters blocked the road in front of Mirpur Bangla College near the Technical intersection.
Job seekers also took to the streets in Motijheel and at the Aarong intersection in Asad Gate, bringing traffic to a standstill in the affected areas.
The protesters questioned why question paper leaks were still occurring under the current government, recalling that such incidents had also taken place under the previous regime. They questioned the significance of the July 2024 uprising, in which thousands of people sacrificed their lives.
They demanded that the government identify those responsible and ensure exemplary punishment, as well as take strict measures to prevent similar incidents in the future.
Afzal Hossain, a job seeker, said he had travelled hundreds of kilometres from a remote area to Dhaka to sit for the examination.
“After enduring so much hardship to reach the exam centre, I learned that the examination had been postponed because the question paper had been leaked,” he said.
“Who will compensate the thousands of us who went to such lengths to sit for the examination? We demand exemplary punishment for everyone involved in the question paper leak,” he added.

item.title: Durga Puja festivities begin with observance of Mahalaya
item.description:
Mahalaya, which marks the beginning of Hindu community’s largest religious festival Durga Puja, is being observed across the country amid festivity on Saturday.
From early morning, temples across the country resonated with Chandipath, tarpan rituals, and devotional hymns in praise of Goddess Durga.
The serene autumn dawn ushered in Devipaksha, the fortnight dedicated to the goddess, through the traditional recitation of sacred verses.
Mahalaya that is considered as ceremonial invocation of goddess Durga is observed seven days prior to the initiation of the Durga Puja, the largest religious festival of the Hindu community.
Hindus believe the earth prepares itself and welcomes the coming of the Goddess and her children, through the celebration.
On this day, Hindus remember and pay homage to the deceased ancestors by performing a puja, and offering Brahmins clothes, food and sweets in their name.
From this day, the countdown to Durga Puja begins.
This year, Shashthi Puja will be celebrated on October 17 while Bijoya Dashami on October 21 will mark the goddess’s departure to Kailash.
Scriptures mention three major milestones of Durga Puja—Mahalaya, Bodhon, and Sandhi Puja. On Mahalaya, Goddess Durga receives the divine mandate to defeat the demon king Mahishasura.
Empowered by the combined forces of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva, she emerges as `Mahashakti’, adorned with ten weapons and riding a lion, ultimately slaying Mahishasura after a nine-day battle.

item.title: Beyond physical relief
item.description:
The global theme for World Hospice and Palliative Care Day 2026, “Pain Management: An Essential Part of Palliative Care,” highlights one of the most profound challenges in modern healthcare: Preventing avoidable suffering and preserving human dignity at every stage of illness.
Pain relief is a fundamental component of compassionate care and a recognized human right. However, in countries like Bangladesh, the challenge extends beyond clinical knowledge -- it involves accessibility, awareness, healthcare infrastructure, cultural understanding, and the ability to provide care that addresses not only disease but also the person experiencing it.
As palliative care practitioners understand, textbooks and clinical guidelines teach us how to assess pain, prescribe analgesics, and manage physical symptoms. Yet, they cannot fully capture the emotional reality of sitting beside a person facing a life-limiting illness.
The deepest lessons often emerge from patients and families -- their courage, their fears, their hopes, and their unwavering desire for comfort and companionship. True palliative care begins when scientific knowledge meets human compassion.
In advanced illnesses such as cancer, pain is rarely limited to physical sensation alone. Dame Cicely Saunders’ concept of “ total pain ” transformed our understanding of suffering by recognizing that pain includes biological, psychological, social, and spiritual dimensions.
A patient may experience physical discomfort, fear of death, anxiety about family responsibilities, financial distress, loneliness, or questions about meaning and purpose. Medicines can control physiological pain, but only compassionate communication, emotional support, and human presence can address the deeper layers of suffering.
This understanding is particularly important in Bangladesh, where the burden of non-communicable diseases continues to increase.
According to WHO estimates, non-communicable diseases account for approximately 63% of all deaths in Bangladesh, with conditions such as cancer, cardiovascular disease, stroke, chronic respiratory disease, and diabetes contributing significantly to mortality.
As the population ages and chronic illnesses become more prevalent, the need for accessible palliative care services is expected to rise substantially.
As per the WHO, Globally, approximately 56.8 million people require palliative care every year, yet only about 14% of those in need receive such services. The majority of this unmet need exists in low- and middle-income countries, including Bangladesh, where healthcare systems often prioritize curative treatment while symptom control and end-of-life support remain underdeveloped.
Bangladesh has made meaningful progress in establishing palliative care services. The Department of Palliative Medicine at Bangladesh Medical University has played a pioneering role in developing institutional and community-based palliative care initiatives. Bangladesh published its National Palliative Care Guideline in 2019, marking an important step toward integrating palliative care into the national healthcare framework.
However, significant challenges remain, including limited trained professionals, inadequate public awareness, insufficient community-based services, and barriers to essential pain medicines.
One of the most critical challenges is access to appropriate pain medication, particularly opioid analgesics such as morphine, which are essential for managing moderate to severe cancer pain.
Evidence from Bangladesh has shown that restricted availability and concerns regarding opioid use have historically contributed to inadequate pain control among patients with advanced cancer.
A study examining morphine use in advanced cancer patients in Bangladesh found that limited access to morphine remained a major barrier to effective pain management, resulting in unnecessary physical suffering and emotional distress for both patients and families.
However, pain management must never be viewed only through the lens of medication. The essence of palliative care lies in restoring dignity and preserving identity when cure is no longer possible.
Dr Harvey Max Chochinov’s work on dignity therapy demonstrated that maintaining a patient’s sense of meaning, identity, and personal value can significantly reduce existential suffering near the end of life.
In Bangladeshi society, where family bonds and spiritual values hold deep importance, the role of family presence becomes especially meaningful.
A gentle touch, sitting beside a loved one, listening without judgment, offering reassurance, or sharing a prayer can provide a level of comfort that medicine alone cannot achieve. These simple acts communicate a powerful message: “You are not alone; you are still valued and loved.”
For many families, end-of-life experiences become lasting memories. Research on communication and bereavement has shown that compassionate conversations, emotional availability, and meaningful interactions between patients, caregivers, and healthcare professionals influence how families process loss. The quality of care provided during the final stages of life can shape memories that remain long after death.
Bangladesh now stands at an important point where palliative care must move beyond specialized hospital units and become integrated into primary healthcare, home-based services, and community health systems.
Training more doctors, nurses, and healthcare workers in pain assessment, symptom management, communication skills, and ethical decision-making is essential.
The WHO emphasizes that palliative care should be incorporated into healthcare systems as a core component of universal health coverage, ensuring that patients receive relief from physical, psychological, social, and spiritual suffering.
Ultimately, World Hospice and Palliative Care Day 2026 reminds us that pain management is not complete when pain scores decrease; it is complete when a person feels heard, respected, and accompanied.
Modern medicine can control symptoms, but compassion gives meaning to care. In the final chapters of life, patients may forget the names of medicines, procedures, and machines, but they remember the presence of those who stood beside them.
For Bangladesh, strengthening palliative care is a reflection of our collective humanity. By combining evidence-based pain management with emotional support, cultural sensitivity, and family-centered care, we can ensure that no person faces serious illness in unnecessary suffering but instead experiences comfort, dignity, and peace.
Sumit Banik is a public health activist and trainer.

item.title: Man City guilty verdict reignites Liverpool rivalry
item.description:
Manchester City will face the full fury of Anfield on Sunday when the Premier League leaders confront old rivals Liverpool in their first game since being found guilty of breaking financial rules.
City can expect a hostile reception from Liverpool fans after an independent commission found they arranged "sham" deals to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than £900 million ($1.2 billion) between 2009 and 2018.
The financial breaches occurred during a period in which City won three Premier League titles and numerous other trophies, with Liverpool struggling to break the Etihad Stadium outfit's silverware monopoly.
City have appealed against the devastating verdict and manager Enzo Maresca was bullish on Friday that they will overturn the original ruling.
But the Premier League season is now stuck in stasis awaiting a ruling on the appeal and any potential sanction.
"I think the worst thing probably is the uncertainty, that no one knows what's going to happen," Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola said on Friday.
A severe points penalty leading to relegation or even expulsion from the English top flight are on the table, while there is also speculation City could be stripped of titles.
"I think they have to be stripped of the titles. Otherwise you send the wrong message to anyone in the future," John Gibbons of Liverpool podcast The Anfield Wrap told AFP.
"There can't be any trust now, certainly not if there's not an admission of guilt. For me, I don't see how Manchester City continue in the league."
Over the past 12 years, Liverpool have finished second to City on three occasions.
Only one of those in 2013/14 came during the period under scrutiny.
But City's rivals believe the wrongdoing in that period built the foundations for a golden era under former boss Pep Guardiola, who stepped down at the end of last season.
- 'Not playing by same rules' -
Twice Jurgen Klopp's Reds missed out on the title despite amassing over 90 points.
Those title battles turned meetings between City and Liverpool into English football's marquee event and the eyes of the world will be on Anfield again come Sunday.
"It just shows how remarkable that team that Jurgen Klopp built was and what they were up against," added Gibbons.
"They were obviously going against another side who it has been shown weren't playing by the same rules as everyone else."
Even in happier times, City have rarely enjoyed their trips to Anfield.
Last season's 2-1 victory was City's first win there in front of a crowd since 2003, with their other win coming amid Covid-19 restrictions in 2021.
City return to Anfield sitting top of the Premier League after a flawless start to Maresca's reign, featuring seven successive wins in all competitions.
Just months after the charges against the club were first announced in February 2023, City went on to win the treble, clinching the club's first Champions League crown, as well as the Premier League and FA Cup.
The question is whether Maresca's men can tap into that siege mentality once more, rather than wilting under the intense scrutiny.
Liverpool supporters have often created a febrile atmosphere for City's visits since they emerged as title contenders following the takeover by their Abu Dhabi-based owners in 2008.
This weekend's showdown is likely to set a new standard for vitriol directed at City's players and fans.
"It's going to be massively hostile," said Dom Farrell, author of the book "Glory Days for the Waifs and Strays" that chronicled City's rise from the third tier to European champions.
"If they were to win against Liverpool and then beat an off-form Paris Saint-Germain you really get a siege mentality going.
"But there's also a decent chance they get turned over and then it just starts to feel you're in this sort of dead zone waiting for the verdict."

item.title: New Zealand paceman O'Rourke to miss India series with injury
item.description:
Injured strike bowler Will O'Rourke has been ruled out of the home series against India and will target a return to face Australia, New Zealand Cricket announced on Saturday.
O'Rourke is recovering from hamstring and calf muscle injuries and will not play in the home ODI and Test matches against India as a "precaution", a statement from the national body said.
New Zealand coach Rob Walter hoped his key new ball bowler would be cleared to play in the four-Test series in Australia starting in early December.
"It's obviously disappointing for Will to have to miss such a marquee tour at home against India," Walter said.
"We all agreed it was best for him to take some more time to rehabilitate both injuries and safely build up his bowling loads.
"Our pace bowling resources will be critical over the next few months so we're taking a conservative approach to Will's return to ensure he's fully fit before he takes the field again."
The 25-year-old has impressed in 14 Tests since his 2024 debut, taking 49 wickets at an average just under 25.
He was a hostile performer in New Zealand's 2-1 series win in England in June, taking 10 wickets, but hasn't played since injuring his hamstring in the final Test.
He subsequently suffered a calf injury at a training session in August.
O'Rourke was previously sidelined for seven months with a back stress fracture before returning to the field earlier this year.
New Zealand have been hit by injuries in the lead-up to India's visit which comprises five Twenty20 Internationals starting on October 22, five ODIs and two Tests.

item.title: Hope, Rutherford lead West Indies to famous victory
item.description:
It was a night of extraordinary hitting in Ranchi as West Indies pulled off a stunning chase of 250, reaching the target in just 18.3 overs. Captain Shai Hope led from the front with a magnificent 102 off 45 balls, while Sherfane Rutherford’s 84 off 37 set the chase alight.
Despite losing two wickets in the opening over, the visitors found their footing quickly and produced a remarkable batting display to level the three-match T20I series 1-1. Only South Africa’s successful chase of 259 against West Indies in 2023 stands higher in men’s T20I history.
"We need to find a way to try and stop the opposition, especially when they lost two wickets in the first over and then lost three in the first six," India head coach Gautam Gambhir said post-match.
"Obviously it was tough. But again, credit to West Indies, the way Sherfane Rutherford and Shai Hope batted. We know that they are world-class batters, especially in this format. So obviously it was tough on us, but we are going to keep improving."
Put in to bat, India made full use of the favourable batting conditions and some wayward bowling to post 249/5, their highest T20I total against West Indies. With dew setting in early and their top order packed with aggressive options, the hosts kept the pressure on the visitors throughout the innings.
After a string of low scores, Sanju Samson rediscovered his touch with a superb 82 off 41 balls. His innings provided the early impetus India needed, as he attacked from the start of the innings and ensured the scoring rate remained high. Ishan Kishan (43 off 22 balls) also made a valuable contribution before his dismissal briefly slowed India's progress.
That lull did not last long. Shreyas Iyer (40 off 18 balls) and Tilak Varma (44 off 18 balls) took charge at the death, combining for an explosive 83-run stand off just 33 balls. Their late assault propelled India towards the 250 mark and left West Indies with a daunting target.
Roston Chase was the standout bowler for the visitors to finish with three wickets. Shamar Springer also picked up two wickets.
West Indies could hardly have made a worse start to the chase. Mayank Yadav struck twice in the opening over, dismissing Kamil Pooran and Shimron Hetmyer off consecutive deliveries to put India firmly on top.
But Hope refused to let the early setbacks dictate the innings. The skipper continued his prolific run of form on tour, finding boundaries regularly and keeping the required rate within reach. Rovman Powell provided valuable support with a brisk 24 off 13 balls, striking at 184.61, as West Indies raced to 72 in the Powerplay. Mayank returned to dismiss Powell, but the hosts were unable to break the momentum.
Sherfane Rutherford joined Hope and immediately shifted the contest into another gear. Taking on both pace and spin, Rutherford unleashed a barrage of boundaries and sixes, putting India’s bowlers under immense pressure. The pair added 120 runs off just 54 balls before Kuldeep Yadav finally broke the partnership by removing Rutherford for a breathtaking 84 off 37 deliveries.
With the chase still demanding a strong finish, Romario Shepherd stepped in at No. 5 after leaving the field with a niggle earlier in the match. His return provided exactly the late-innings boost West Indies needed, as he smashed an unbeaten 34 off just 13 balls, including three fours and three sixes.
At the other end, Hope continued to dictate terms. He brought up his century in just 45 balls, capping a remarkable innings with a six over wide long-on. His unbeaten 102 off 45 deliveries featured a relentless mix of power and placement, ensuring the target was reached with 9 balls to spare.
West Indies finished on 253/4 in 18.3 overs, completing the second-highest successful chase in men’s T20I cricket and registering their highest successful run chase in the format.
Having chased down 352 against India in New Chandigarh earlier in the tour to record their highest successful ODI chase, West Indies delivered another remarkable run chase in Ranchi. With Hope once again at the heart of the performance, the visitors levelled the T20I series at 1-1 to now move to Indore for the third T20I on 11 October.

item.title: Our roads need better planning
item.description:
The inauguration of Bangladesh’s first dedicated cycle track in Chittagong is a welcome step towards safer, more sustainable urban transport. Stretching 2.2 kilometres, the new facility demonstrates how road infrastructure can be designed to accommodate cyclists and pedestrians alongside motorized traffic.
However, this initiative must be the beginning of a broader shift in how we plan our roads.
In Bangladesh, road planning has long prioritized the movement of motor vehicles, often at the expense of pedestrians, cyclists, and public transport users. In crowded cities such as Dhaka and Chittagong, this imbalance contributes to congestion, unsafe journeys, and an urban environment that discourages walking and cycling.
Dedicated cycling or bike lanes should, therefore, be introduced across major urban roads wherever feasible, with physical barriers and clear markings to prevent other vehicles from encroaching on them.
Equally important are dedicated bus lanes that allow public transport to move efficiently without being trapped in the same congestion as private cars.
Better bus services, reliable schedules, and safe boarding facilities would encourage more people to choose public transport, reducing the number of private vehicles on the roads.
These measures must be supported by comprehensive planning, and road projects must also account for drainage, roadside activity, and connections between different modes of transport instead of treating each development as an isolated undertaking.
The authorities must ensure that these facilities are maintained, kept free from illegal parking and encroachment, and supported by consistent enforcement of traffic laws.
Chittagong’s new cycle track offers a practical example of what better road design can achieve. The challenge now is to replicate -- and also improve upon -- this approach nationwide.
Our roads should not merely move vehicles faster; they must enable everyone to travel safely, comfortably, and affordably. Better road planning must be treated as a necessity for a safer, more liveable Bangladesh.

item.title: Mental health is health
item.description:
World Mental Health Day, observed on October 10, serves as an important reminder that mental health deserves more attention.
In Bangladesh, however, it remains an issue that is too often discussed in whispers, dismissed as weakness, or ignored until a crisis makes it impossible to overlook.
This silence must end if we are serious about building a healthier nation.
The pressures of modern life are taking a toll on people across all age groups. Financial insecurity, academic expectations, workplace stress, family conflicts, and uncertainty about the future can affect anyone.
Yet, many people in Bangladesh hesitate to seek help because they fear judgement, social stigma, or being misunderstood.
Mental health struggles are frequently met with advice to remain strong, pray harder, or simply move on, as though distress can be overcome through willpower alone.
Changing this reality requires sustained action. Mental health education must become a part of schools and workplaces, helping people recognize distress and understand when professional support is necessary. Affordable counselling and psychiatric services must be made more accessible, particularly outside major cities.
The government must also invest in trained professionals, strengthen community-based services, and ensure that mental healthcare receives adequate funding and policy attention.
Equally important is the role of families, educators, employers, and the media in creating environments where people can speak without fear of ridicule or discrimination. Seeking help must be treated as a responsible decision, not a source of shame.
This World Mental Health Day should be more than an annual observance marked by statements and awareness campaigns. It should encourage lasting changes in how we understand and respond to psychological distress.
It is time we accept this simple truth: Shying away from mental health issues will never create a healthy nation. We must start talking, listening, and acting -- before silence causes further harm.

item.title: Barrister Abdul Muntaquim Chaudhury dies at 97
item.description:
Barrister Abdul Muntaquim Chaudhury, a Bangladeshi politician, lawyer and organizer of the Liberation War, died in Melbourne, Australia, on October 9, 2026. He was 97.
Born on September 2, 1929, Chaudhury served as a member of Pakistan’s National Assembly in the 1960s and was re-elected in 1970. After Bangladesh gained independence, he became a member of the Constituent Assembly and helped draft the country’s constitution.
In 1973, he was appointed Bangladesh’s ambassador to Japan. He later served as the country’s ambassador to the German Democratic Republic.
After returning to Bangladesh in 1979, Chaudhury became the founding executive director of the Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (Blast).
Abu Taher Abdul Muntaquim Chaudhury, whose family descended from the Kanihati Chaudhury family of Sylhet, was the youngest child of Khan Bahadur Tazzammul Ali Chaudhury.
He completed his Intermediate of Arts (IA) at Aligarh Muslim University before studying at Santiniketan and St Xavier’s College. He earned his bachelor’s degree from the University of Calcutta and was later called to the bar at Lincoln’s Inn in London.

India 'cockroach' movement says thousands detained during major protest in capital
item.description:
TOPSHOT-INDIA-POLITICS-PROTEST

Indian police detained the head of the satirical "cockroach" online movement as well as thousands of protesters trying to take part in a major demonstration in New Delhi against the country's election commissioner, the group said on Saturday.

The protest is the culmination of weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter-roll revision by the Election Commission of India (ECI).

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke and two other leaders were detained before disembarking from a flight in the capital, according to a statement from the group.

"They're being denied access to their lawyers and cut off from all contact with others," it said, adding the trio had been taken to "an undisclosed location".

The CJP also said that thousands more protesters were detained in New Delhi as they attempted to march to the main Jantar Mantar protest site, defying a massive security clampdown.

"More than 15,000 protesters have been detained," Ajinkya Shinde, a CJP leader, said at a news conference in Delhi.

Police did not immediately respond to AFP's request for comment on detentions.

"We will be back, let them fill up all the jails," Shinde said.

Dhruv Rathee arrested over Jantar Mantar protest

Dozens of protesters shouted anti-government slogans as they were taken away in police vehicles, AFP reporters witnessed.

Calls for the ECI chief Gyanesh Kumar to step down have intensified in recent weeks as opposition parties and critics said his commission's voter-roll revision could disenfranchise millions of constituents and benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.

The ECI has rejected allegations of impropriety, saying the revision was intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters.

Ahead of the protest, authorities in the capital deployed thousands of police, closed dozens of metro stations, cancelled more than 200 trains and temporarily shut down mobile internet around the protest site.

The demonstrations are widely seen as a reprise of the "cockroach" movement's mass mobilisation in July, which led to the education minister stepping down over an examination scandal.

This time, protesters are demanding Kumar's resignation and a halt to the voter revision exercise.

Fresh challenge

The accusations are a fresh challenge for 76-year-old Modi during his third term in office.

Opposition parties have long alleged that legitimate voters are being struck off lists in India, the world's largest democracy with 1.4 billion people.

The issue flared up last month when the Indian Express newspaper reported that key decisions linked to the revision were likely taken without the approval of two of the three election commissioners.

The ECI, a constitutional body, says all its decisions were unanimous and legally valid.

Demonstrators expressed anger on Saturday, telling AFP their right to protest peacefully was being hampered.

Saransh, a university graduate, walked several miles after navigating security barricades to get close to the Jantar Mantar protest site.

"I am here to protect the constitution," said the 24-year-old, who gave only one name.

"Why do I need permission to peacefully express my opinion?"

'Keep protesting'

Amnesty International denounced the "lockdown-like restrictions" and leader of the opposition Congress party, Rahul Gandhi, called on young people to continue with the rallies.

"Youth of India, I am proud of you. Keep protesting. We are standing with you," he said.

The Hindu newspaper reported more than 5,000 protesters had been detained, although it was not immediately possible to verify that number.

Media outlets, including the Scroll and Newslaundry, said their journalists had also been detained briefly.

The United Nations' human rights office urged India to release those "arbitrarily detained" in the protests and expressed concern at reports of mass detentions.

BJP spokesman Sambit Patra said on Saturday the CJP had failed in its attempt to spread "anarchy".

"What is happening at Jantar Mantar, what you can see on TV and a few social media handles, is not India's story," he told reporters.

The voter list overhaul, which began in 2025, has led to more than 133 million names being excluded from draft rolls, according to Indian media reports citing ECI data.

Mamata, Kejriwal and Dipke among hundreds detained, Delhi locked down to foil protest

The ECI has said the voter-roll revision identifies fraudulently registered voters and aims to prevent "foreign illegal immigrants" from voting.

Critics say the drive has disproportionately affected marginalised and minority communities.

Members of Modi's party have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India's electoral rolls.

Political analyst Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay told AFP the protest comes at a time when Modi appears to be "at his weakest politically and individually".

Though India's next general elections are not slated until 2029, the country's most populous state of Uttar Pradesh will go to the polls next year.

"I see this becoming a bigger challenge in the coming months," Mukhopadhyay said.

item.title: Tarique Rahman calls sudden BNP parliamentary party meeting
item.description:
Although the date for the next session of parliament has not yet been set, leader of the House and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has unexpectedly called a meeting of the BNP parliamentary party.

The meeting will be held at 6pm tomorrow, Sunday, in the ruling party's meeting room at the Jatiya Sangsad.

Several senior BNP leaders said the meeting may discuss establishing discipline within the party, the recent law and order situation, constitutional amendments and the upcoming local government elections.

Parliamentary party meetings are usually held one or two days before a parliamentary session begins or during the session. This time, however, the meeting has been called before the date of the next session has been determined. The next session of parliament may begin in the second week of November.

BNP leaders believe the decision to call the meeting outside the regular schedule reflects the need to provide lawmakers with guidance on several important issues. A senior party leader, speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, said, “The prime minister has called everyone. He will surely give instructions on some important and urgent issues.”

People familiar with the matter said BNP leaders see a need to discuss internal party discipline, the law and order situation, and upcoming political and organisational challenges, which may explain why the meeting has been called outside the regular schedule of parliamentary party meetings.

Speaking to several senior BNP leaders, Prothom Alo learned that the meeting will discuss the overall political situation. Allegations of land grabbing, extortion and irregularities against party leaders and activists in recent times, the law and order situation, constitutional amendments and the upcoming local government elections may feature on the agenda. The meeting may also provide guidance on organisational matters.

Law and order and constitutional amendments

The law and order situation and allegations that party leaders and activists are involved in criminal activities have become important political issues for the ruling party.

A recent example is the attack and vandalism at Radda, a private healthcare centre in Mirpur, Dhaka. BNP lawmaker Ferdousi Ahmed Misti, who represents a reserved seat for women, resigned following the incident. The allegations against her are under investigation. Following the incident, three committees, including the Dhaka North City BNP committee, were dissolved, and 14 party leaders and activists at various levels were expelled.

Through these measures, the BNP has sent a message that it will take action against individuals involved in land grabbing, extortion and violence under the cover of their party affiliation.

Constitutional amendments are also an important issue for the government. A special committee of parliament is working on proposals to implement the July National Charter and reform the Constitution.

Home Affairs Minister and committee chairman Salahuddin Ahmed said on 20 September that the committee aimed to conclude discussions and submit a report to parliament by December. Political parties, constitutional experts and other stakeholders are also expected to be consulted.

Political consensus may become crucial in implementing the charter's proposals, determining the opposition's role in parliament and reforming state institutions as part of the constitutional amendment process. The parliamentary party meeting may provide guidance on the BNP's position on these issues and what lawmakers should do.

Local elections and party organisation

The upcoming local government elections will also be a major organisational test for the BNP. Following the national election, the party faces several challenges at the local level, including managing grassroots expectations and grievances over the selection of local representatives, controlling competition among potential candidates and selecting candidates who are broadly acceptable.

Amid uncertainty over the election schedule and preparations, central party directives may help shape the position of grassroots leaders and activists.

In addition to running the government, the BNP must keep its organisational activities functioning after coming to power. Party sources believe the meeting may also discuss restructuring committees, deciding the fate of committees whose terms have expired, and maintaining discipline among party leaders and activists.

item.title: Evacuations, injuries at Riyadh airport after alleged Houthi attack
item.description:
IRAN-CRISIS/SAUDI-AIRPORT

Yemen's Houthis attacked Riyadh's international airport with a missile on Saturday, a diplomatic source told AFP, with dozens reported wounded and a witness describing panic in the terminal.

Saudi authorities did not confirm any new attack or evacuation, but one witness reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded.

"I was on gate 403" at the domestic terminal, the witness told AFP.

"I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."

A source at a local hospital told AFP that five people were in intensive care after being wounded at the airport, saying "dozens of people were injured" in all.

The relative of one injured person said they had been wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass, and had been taken to hospital.

Three witnesses confirmed people being evacuated from the airport.

"Houthis are attacking civilian targets. Riyadh airport is a civilian target," the diplomatic source told AFP, saying the airport was hit by "a missile around 3:00 pm" (1200 GMT).

The airport was hit by deadly attacks claimed by Yemen's Houthis on Thursday, though the Iran-backed group did not announce any fresh strikes on the facility on Saturday.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.

Saudi Arabia says 3 dead at airports after Houthis claim attacks

Admissions by Saudi authorities of strikes hitting civilian targets are relatively rare, with officials issuing few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.

The scale and frequency of the recent strikes targeting Riyadh are unprecedented in the eight months of war that has spread across the Middle East.

Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that supports Yemen's government militarily, and has found itself drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbour's civil war.

Both Riyadh and the Houthis have signalling a willingness to keep fighting rather than pursue diplomacy.

'Contact your airline'

Earlier on Saturday, Riyadh airport urged passengers to check their flight status before coming -- echoing an advisory sent on Thursday, when attacks killed three people including a pilot for Saudia, the national airline.

"Please contact your airline directly and confirm your flight status before heading to the airport," read a statement posted on the airport's official X account on Saturday.

Thursday's Houthi-claimed attacks also badly damaged a grounded Saudia plane.

Meanwhile, in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas they captured last month around the Bab al-Mandab strait, military sources told AFP.

The Yemeni government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the group seized the country's entire western coastline in a lightning offensive.

The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandab area -- a key chokepoint for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping -- but they claimed to have repelled the assault.

Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

item.title: Return of poverty: Where are gaps in the development narrative?
item.description:
The success in poverty reduction in Bangladesh was once one of the strongest examples in development discussions. For many years, a positive relationship was observed between growth, exports, remittances, and improvements in social indicators with poverty reduction.

However, recent trends show a clear disruption in this continuity. According to the World Bank, the poverty rate in the country has increased for four consecutive years. During this period, approximately 8 million people have fallen below the poverty line. Additionally, around 61. 25 million people are in such a vulnerable position.

The economy has grown, but the question of how widely the benefits of that growth have reached people in terms of income, employment and security can no longer be ignored. Over the past few years, high inflation has been one of the major blows to low- and middle-income people. In particular, food inflation has quickly eroded the real income of poor families.

Higher-income families can cope with inflation by reducing some savings or changing spending patterns. Poor families cannot. For them, rising prices mean less food, less nutrition, delaying medical treatment, cutting back on children's education expenses, or relying on debt. Thus, inflation is not just a macroeconomic problem, but it also directly relates to poverty and inequality.

The weaknesses in the labour market have deepened this pressure. Most employment in Bangladesh is still in the informal sector, where job security is low, wages are low, and social insurance is almost non-existent. Even though nominal wages have increased slightly, they have not kept pace with inflation for a long time. As a result, real income has decreased. On the other hand, due to weak private investment, new and quality jobs have not been created sufficiently. Families are thus caught under the pressure of high prices on the one hand and limited income opportunities on the other.

Here, questions about the quality of growth arise. If growth increases production but not employment, its capacity to reduce poverty becomes limited. This disconnect has become more evident in Bangladesh in recent years. A large segment of educated youth is not getting good jobs.

Progress in women's employment has stalled. Small and medium enterprises are struggling under the pressure of loans, energy, markets, and uncertain demand. As a result, families that have risen slightly above poverty are not able to stay in a stable and safe position permanently.

The risk posed to 61. 25 million people is a bigger warning sign. Being above the poverty line and economic security are not the same thing. Illness, job loss, floods, crop failure, new spikes in food prices, or increases in rent and education expenses can completely change a family's position. If this vast population is kept invisible in policy decisions, previous achievements in poverty reduction will not be sustainable.

Yet, Bangladesh's social protection system is still not aligned with this reality. It largely depends on allowances and fragmented programmes. There is some assistance after becoming poor, but the structure to protect people from falling into poverty is weak. There is no unemployment insurance, insufficient financial protection against health expenses, and limited social insurance for informal workers. As a result, families have to bear the risk instead of the state.

Here, the problem is not just a lack of funds. A major issue is institutional weakness. There are errors in selecting beneficiaries, genuine poor are left out, and influential or non-priority people get benefits. Political influence at the local level, weak information systems, limited oversight, and lack of effective grievance redress reduce programme outcomes. Even if the social protection budget is large, its effectiveness does not always increase proportionately.

A tougher question is the political economy. For many years, Bangladesh's economic policy has been run within a framework where organised and influential groups can extract special privileges from policies, but the bargaining power of ordinary people is limited.

In the banking sector, large debt defaulters repeatedly get waivers. Some sectors get tax exemptions or protection. On the other hand, if a worker loses a job or a small business loses capital, there is no comparatively strong protection for them. This means the distribution of risk is uneven. The state often bears the cost of failures of powerful groups, but the failures of ordinary people remain personal. This framework gradually shifts resources and opportunities towards powerful groups, while weaker families become more insecure.

Market weaknesses are another reason for rising poverty. Questions about the effectiveness of competition in various tiers of food products, transportation, imports, energy, and wholesale trade have persisted for a long time. Even if prices decrease in the international market, the benefits often do not fully reach consumers, but when prices rise, the additional costs are quickly passed downward. This price disparity reflects the power dynamics in the market.

Government responses are often short-term. Market operations, fines, or administrative directives may come into discussion for a while, but they do not solve structural problems. What is needed is an effective role for the competition commission, transparency of market information, monitoring of the import and supply chains, and regulation sufficiently independent of political and business influence.

The tax system also features similar inequities. Excessive reliance on indirect taxes places a comparatively higher burden on low- and middle-income people. In contrast, potential revenue from high income, wealth, capital gains, and various privileged groups is not fully realised. Tax evasion, exemptions, and special privileges reduce revenue capacity. This has a direct impact on health, education, social protection, and urban services.

Therefore, questions of policy prioritisation are also crucial. Large infrastructure projects are politically visible. A bridge, highway, or mega-project easily becomes a symbol of development. However, the income security of a worker, the health protection of a family, or the opportunity for quality education for a child is not visible. Political incentives often prioritise expenditures that can be shown immediately, while sectors that build long-term security for people lag behind.

So now, merely expanding poverty programmes will not suffice. The first task is to see inflation control as a comprehensive economic governance question. Food supply, market competition, import policy, energy prices, transportation costs, and monetary policy need to be looked at together.

Secondly, social protection needs to move beyond allowance limits towards social insurance, unemployment risk, health expenses, and countering income loss. Thirdly, private investment and productive employment need to be brought back to the central strategy for poverty reduction.

In conclusion, the descent of 8 million people into poverty and the vulnerability of 61. 25 million people is not a minor policy deviation. It is a serious warning for our development strategy. If growth does not secure people''s income, improve job quality, and protect families from economic shocks, then the social foundation of that growth will remain weak. Development success becomes meaningful only when people not only rise above the poverty line but also achieve the capability to stay there.
