item.title: Waliullah, away from home
item.description:
Few Bangla writers smell of the soil the way Syed Waliullah does. I knew it when I read his book for the first time.
Ekti Tulsi Gachher Kahini pulled me in so deep that I read one Waliullah book after another and looked nowhere else. In college, Lalsalu turned up on the supplementary reading list, but it never felt like homework. It was uncomfortably familiar, as if someone had pointed at the things society kept quiet about and refused to look away. Then the Bishwo Sahitya Kendra mobile library rolled into my life and handed me Nayanchara and Kando Nadi Kando.
By the time I closed them, I wasn’t only curious about the books anymore. I wanted to know the man.
One image of Waliullah has stayed with me. It comes from Amar Swami Wali , written by his wife, Anne-Marie Waliullah. Picture him on the balcony of their apartment in Meudon, near Paris. Waliullah would gaze at the distant, mist-covered Seine and yearn for his golden Bengal. Perhaps, as he moved through the streets of Karachi, Delhi, Sydney, and Paris, he was quietly weaving stories about some unfamiliar village on the far edges of Bengal.
He even sold his expensive Fiat and bought land in Dhaka. He was ready to go home. But fate did not allow him to return.
At twelve, Waliullah dreamed of becoming a pilot, of rising above the borders of his country altogether. The dream never took off, but the leaving did. He went abroad, made a life there, and fell in love with a foreign woman. In the end, it was that love that kept him from coming home.
His life abroad began in 1951, when he joined the Pakistan government as a press attaché. Postings followed: Delhi, Sydney, Jakarta, London, and finally Paris. Syed Waliullah and his wife Anne-Marie. Photo: Collected.
Between 1952 and 1954, Waliullah served as press attaché at the Pakistan embassy in Sydney. There he met Anne-Marie, who worked at the French consulate.
It was, by all accounts, a love that began at first sight.
What began in Sydney grew into something deeper. After a long courtship, Anne-Marie and Waliullah were married in Karachi in October 1955.
That Waliullah had chosen the right partner became clear in Anne-Marie’s own work. She translated his Lalsalu into French as L’Arbre sans racines . She later translated Chander Amaboshya as Black Moon .
Perhaps Waliullah would have gone home had he not fallen in love with Anne-Marie. But maybe staying abroad was not such a loss. Their love built a bond between Bengal and the French language.
Through that bond, Bangla literature found roots in another language and another culture.
Waliullah was deeply immersed in his own private world. Cinema and concerts with his children were part of his routine. In their elegant apartment in Meudon, on the outskirts of Paris, he and Anne-Marie built a quiet, artistic life with their two children, Simin and Iraj.
I often compare Waliullah’s life to that of filmmaker Tareque Masud. Both married foreign women. Both found partners who backed their work and ideas. Catherine Masud was a source of inspiration for Tareque, including his lifelong engagement with Kagojer Phool . In the same way, Anne-Marie became an important source of inspiration for Waliullah’s literary work and, later, his efforts during the Liberation War.
Waliullah did not express himself only through writing. He was just as passionate about designing furniture with his own hands, painting, designing book covers, and working as a carpenter.
According to his son Iraj, Waliullah came home at night with small gifts for his children. Sometimes there were sarees for Anne-Marie. He loved to cook, especially shami kebabs and chapatis. At home, he wore the traditional Bengali lungi.
Even on foreign soil, Syed Waliullah lived an unmistakably Bengali life.
What fascinated me most was learning about the circle of friends he built in exile.
Bengalis regularly gathered at his Paris home. The apartment gave Waliullah a small breathing space of Bangladesh. The doors stayed open to any Bengali arriving in France. Waliullah himself would take visitors to the Louvre or the Palace of Versailles. Over conversations with friends, Bengali food and musical gatherings, a little piece of Bangladesh was recreated in the heart of Paris.
The home welcomed people such as sculptor Novera Ahmed, artist Rashid Choudhury, Nazmuddin Hashim, and Humayun Rashid Chowdhury. Waliullah would even cook for his guests.
Waliullah’s circle was not limited to Bengalis. Friends from Karachi also visited his Paris apartment. Among them was the celebrated Urdu novelist Qurratul-ain Hyder, along with several progressive non-Bengali intellectuals and writers.
Then came 1971, and everything changed.
The Waliullah family in the Alps, 1964. Photo Collected.
The Liberation War came closer, step by step. From Paris, Waliullah and Anne-Marie worked tirelessly to build international support for Bangladesh. A second war had begun, this time on foreign soil.
Long before the war, Waliullah had planted the seeds of the struggle for self-determination in Ekti Tulsi Gachher Kahini. When it began, he joined the cause on his own initiative.
Two months after Waliullah’s death, in December 1971, French citizen Jean Kay became widely known for hijacking an aircraft in support of Bangladesh’s independence. Away from the limelight, Anne-Marie Thibault had quietly worked alongside Waliullah for the same cause.
Then the pressure came from Pakistan. His contract with UNESCO in Paris was nearing its end, and the Pakistan government ordered him to return to Karachi or Islamabad.
But how could he obey a state whose forces were killing his own people? He resigned. His secure income vanished. Severe financial hardship followed. Yet he did not move an inch from his decision to fight for the independence of his homeland.
Jobless and uncertain about money, Waliullah became one of the voices of the Liberation War abroad. He worked alongside his friend, Justice Abu Sayeed Chowdhury, and threw himself into building support across Europe.
He went from door to door among leading French intellectuals such as Pierre Emmanuel and André Malraux, trying to turn French public opinion towards Bangladesh. He pledged his allegiance to the provisional government of Bangladesh and raised funds tirelessly.
Anne-Marie stood beside him, carrying the message of the Liberation War to the French media.
Uncertainty about his homeland. Anxiety over its future. Exhaustion of body and mind. Slowly, all of it wore down Waliullah’s health. He longed to return to an independent Bangladesh and had already bought property in Dhaka.
But he never got to see the red sun of an independent Bangladesh.
He died on October 10, 1971, just two months before the emergence of an independent and sovereign Bangladesh. A cerebral hemorrhage took the legendary Bangla writer at his home in Meudon, near Paris.
Today he lies peacefully in a quiet cemetery in a village of Meudon, near Paris.
If he had a grave in Dhaka, I would visit it at least once.
The man who wrote about the soil of Bengal, whose writing was so deeply rooted in its people, may have gone years without hearing Bangla. And now he is not here to hear it.
Perhaps once exile pulls someone away, they lose the freedom to answer the call of their mother’s embrace.
Sherrif Faruqi is a short story writer and journalist at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Two Biman employees confess in Tk16.25 crore gold smuggling case
item.description:
Two employees of Biman Bangladesh Airlines have given confessional statements before a court in a case over the recovery of 80 gold bars worth an estimated Tk16.25 crore from their shoes at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka.
Manik Mia and Mizanur Rahman were produced before the court on Saturday after completing a five-day remand. As they agreed to make confessional statements voluntarily, the case’s investigating officer, Airport Police Station Inspector Abul Qaiyum, applied to have their statements recorded.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Hasan Shahadat recorded their statements and later ordered that they be sent to jail, said Abu Bakar Siddique, a sub-inspector of the police prosecution division.
The Customs Intelligence and Investigation Directorate (CIID) announced the detention of the two Biman employees on Sunday morning. The following day, a court granted five days of remand for their interrogation.
According to a CIID press release, officials took up positions at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on Sunday following a tip-off. They recovered 80 gold bars concealed inside the employees’ shoes near the runway where Emirates Airlines flight EK-0582 from Dubai was stationed.
Each bar weighed approximately 117 grams, bringing the total weight of the seized gold to around 9.34kg. The estimated market value was Tk16.25 crore.
The CIID said it was investigating the source of the gold, the intended recipients and others involved in the alleged smuggling operation.
On Sunday, Ruhani Islam, an assistant revenue officer of the airport’s Customs Intelligence and Investigation Circle, filed a case under the Special Powers Act over the incident.

item.title: DU teacher seeks chance to explain niqab remarks, calls for probe
item.description:
Dhaka University English department Associate Professor Tasneem Siraj Mahboob has sought an opportunity to explain her remarks about a niqab-wearing student in a classroom and called for an impartial investigation, while expressing concern over threats and harassment following the incident.
In a written statement read out during a Facebook Live session on her page on Saturday afternoon, she said she wanted the university authorities to hear her explanation and examine statements from all concerned before reaching a decision.
Tasneem said the incident occurred during a master's final semester class on October 7, when she had difficulty immediately identifying a student whose entire face, including her eyes, was covered. The lack of eye contact, she said, made it difficult to understand how the student was receiving her remarks and participating in classroom activities.
She said she raised the issue because she did not feel comfortable teaching under those circumstances.
Tasneem said she had upheld religious values and observances throughout her nearly 34-year teaching career and denied intending to insult any student's religious beliefs or clothing.
Explaining her discussion of Islamic rules on veiling, she said that, based on her understanding after reading translations of the Quran, women could wear modest clothing that did not reveal their body shape while keeping their faces visible. She also referred to religious interpretations and a hadith concerning women not wearing niqabs while in the state of ihram during Hajj.
She claimed she had not instructed the student to change her clothes, remove her niqab or leave the classroom. She also said the student had not been punished for wearing religious clothing or barred from attending future classes.
According to Tasneem, her remarks concerned the difficulty of identifying the student because her eyes were covered.
She said that after the student left the classroom, she learned from classmates that her remarks had hurt the student. She then sent messages through classmates on 3 occasions expressing a wish to apologize and waited in the corridor for about 10 minutes, but the student did not come to speak with her, preventing a direct apology.
Tasneem also said she had to leave for the hospital urgently on the day of the incident because a family member was seriously ill and undergoing surgery. During that time, she learned that her remarks were being circulated in a distorted form.
Regarding the English department's response, she said all her courses had been distributed among other teachers based on students' written complaints without her statement being heard. She said she was distressed that the decision had been made before she had an opportunity to explain her position.
She called for an impartial examination of the incident based on statements from all concerned and relevant information, adding that she was prepared to cooperate with the process.
Expressing concern for her personal safety, Tasneem said she had received anonymous phone calls, emails, offensive messages and threats following the incident. She sought the university authorities' assistance in ensuring the dignity and safety of everyone involved, including the student, and preventing threats and harassment.
Earlier, on Thursday, a group of female students from the English department submitted a written complaint about the incident to the university's proctor and Pro-Vice-Chancellor (Administration), Professor Dr Mohammed Almujaddade Alfasane.
In their complaint, the students demanded an impartial investigation and the permanent expulsion of Tasneem from the university if the allegations were proven. They also sought an unconditional apology to students of the batch concerned and her removal from teaching and academic assessment involving those students.
The students further called for measures to ensure that no student suffered academic harm, harassment or retaliation.
Subsequently, activists of the Dhaka University branch of Bangladesh Islami Chhatri Sangstha held a human chain at the foot of the Raju Sculpture, demanding legal action against the teacher.
English department Chairperson Dr Tazin Aziz Chaudhury said an emergency academic committee meeting had been held following the students' written complaints. According to the meeting's decision, Tasneem's courses had been distributed among other teachers, and she would not be allowed to conduct classes for any course for the time being.
In her statement, Tasneem said classrooms should be respectful and safe spaces for both teachers and students. She added that when identity verification was necessary, it should be carried out under clear institutional policies that respected religious beliefs, personal dignity and privacy.

item.title: Kejriwal detained ahead of CJP protest in Delhi
item.description:
Former Delhi chief minister and Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) national convenor Arvind Kejriwal was detained by Delhi Police on Saturday while marching towards Jantar Mantar to join a protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter roll irregularities.
The detention came amid a heavy security deployment across central Delhi ahead of a demonstration led by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), which has accused the election authorities of involvement in alleged “vote theft.”
Kejriwal had criticized the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led central government earlier in the day, describing the security crackdown as “worse than Emergency” and condemning the detention of CJP leaders.
“Three-time Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal brutally taken into custody by Delhi Police, for demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation,” senior AAP leader Atishi said in a post on X.
“Modi Ji: how many people will you put behind bars to save Gyanesh Kumar?” she added.
On Friday, Kejriwal had announced that he and his family would attend the protest, urging young people to join the demonstration seeking Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in voter lists.
Following the detention of CJP leaders on Saturday morning, Kejriwal said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had shown that he was “scared” by arresting the protesters, whom he referred to as “cockroaches.”
Meanwhile, the AAP alleged that police had turned Kejriwal’s residence into a fortress ahead of the protest.
Delhi unit president Bharadwaj said the demonstrators wanted to raise their concerns peacefully, but the heavy deployment of security personnel was creating an atmosphere of fear.
“You cannot make Gen-Z keep quiet by force — these are our youth; talk to them, engage with them,” Bharadwaj said in a video message.
He added that India should uphold non-violence and the Constitution rather than create an atmosphere of fear.
Authorities deployed thousands of security personnel across central Delhi to prevent clashes and detain protesters or discourage them from reaching Jantar Mantar.
The Delhi Metro also suspended entry and exit services at 45 stations from 9pm on Friday until 6pm on Saturday as part of the security measures.

item.title: Four held over defacing of Tagore graffiti in Dhaka
item.description:
Police have detained four people, including a woman, over the defacement of a graffiti of Nobel laureate poet Rabindranath Tagore outside the Shilpakala Academy in Dhaka. They are being interrogated by the Detective Branch (DB) of police.
Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) Ramna Division Deputy Commissioner Sheikh Zahidul Islam confirmed the matter to the Dhaka Tribune on Saturday evening.
“Four people, including a woman, have been detained. They are now at the DB for questioning. Their names and identities cannot be disclosed at this stage in the interest of the investigation,” he said.
Earlier on Saturday, Shahbagh police detained A N M Ayas, member secretary of the Rashtra Sanglap Forum, in connection with the incident. Two other people, including a woman, were also detained at the same reason.
The incident, which took place in Segunbagicha ahead of Sharadiya Durga Puja, has raised concerns over the possibility of unrest during the religious festival. However, police have yet to establish whether the defacement was linked to any planned provocation.
Several videos circulating on social media show a woman using a brush to smear black ink on Tagore’s mural. A police officer from Shahbagh Police Station intervened and moved her away from the spot. Following a commotion involving the woman and her associates, police detained them and took them away in a van. They were heard chanting slogans during the incident.
Speaking to the media initially, the woman claimed Tagore had opposed the establishment of the University of Dhaka and had asked, “What need do paupers have of education?” Describing the poet as “against Bangladesh”, she said she had defaced the portrait in protest.
However, she later offered a different account, claiming she had been suffering from a fever and had gone to the Shilpakala Academy area under the pretext of attending a regular protest programme. She said she had not known beforehand that ink would be applied to Tagore’s portrait. She also alleged that a male police officer had pushed her during her detention.
The wall outside the Shilpakala Academy features portraits of several prominent figures from the subcontinent, including Tagore, filmmaker Satyajit Ray, educationist Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar and writer Sanjib Chattopadhyay.
On October 5, following a drive by Dhaka South City Corporation to clear footpath encroachments in Segunbagicha, portraits of 10 eminent figures, including Tagore, Kazi Nazrul Islam, Shilpacharya Zainul Abedin and Satyajit Ray, were painted on the walls. Tagore’s portrait was defaced with ink within days.
Security has been tightened across the capital ahead of Durga Puja. On October 6, DMP Commissioner Mosleh Uddin Ahmed described this year’s festival as an “acid test” for police, pledging maximum security at puja mandaps through the deployment of uniformed and plainclothes officers.

item.title: Comilla schoolgirl murder: Accused CNG driver taken to court for confessional statement
item.description:
A CNG driver arrested in connection with the rape and murder of a Class 7 student in Lalmai, Comilla, was taken to court on Saturday at 3:30pm to record his confessional statement under Section 164.
The accused, identified as Sumon, 35, was produced before Judge Muminul Hoque at Comilla Senior Judicial Magistrate Court No 6.
Comilla Additional Superintendent of Police (Crime) Pankaj Barua said the preliminary police investigation had found information indicating Sumon's sole involvement in the incident.
According to police, Sumon picked up the girl in a CNG from the Paduar Bazar Biswa Road area on Wednesday night, promising to take her home for a fare of Tk300. Police allege that he later took her to a cropland in Lalmai, where he raped and murdered her.
After the murder, Sumon fled to Chittagong with the girl's mobile phone. He was arrested on Friday.
Based on information provided by Sumon, police later recovered the phone from a wooded area in Bakhrabad.
The girl's body was recovered on Thursday morning from a cropland in Jagatpur village under Perul North Union in Lalmai.
She was an irregular Class 7 student at Farida Bidyayatan High School in Comilla city. Her home district was Jeshore, and she lived with her family in the city's Racecourse area.

item.title: UN report identifies key barriers to adolescent sexual health care in Asia-Pacific
item.description:
Financial hardship, legal restrictions and gaps in health services are preventing adolescents across Asia and the Pacific from accessing essential sexual and reproductive health care, according to a United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) report.
Titled 650 Million Reasons: Achieving Universal Health Coverage for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health in Asia and the Pacific, the report examines policies, laws and health data across 30 low- and middle-income countries. Developed with the Burnet Institute, it finds that services remain fragmented and underfunded despite widespread policy commitments, leaving many adolescents without essential information, protection and care.
Asia and the Pacific is home to nearly 650 million adolescents aged 10–19, almost half the world's total. The report says meeting their health needs is essential to achieving universal health coverage, which ensures everyone can access quality health services without financial hardship.
According to the findings, up to 65% of adolescent girls in countries with available data report financial difficulties accessing health care. An average gap of 3 years separates the legal age of consent to sex from the legal age of consent to health care, while only 9 of the 30 countries provide clear guidance on accessing contraception without parental consent.
In most countries covered by the report, fewer than half of sexually active adolescent girls who need family planning services are able to use contraception.
The report also identifies judgmental treatment, discrimination and concerns about privacy as barriers to care. Even when services are free, transportation costs, informal fees and uncertainty about entitlements can prevent adolescents from seeking help.
“For an adolescent who cannot afford care or is turned away because of their age or marital status, a policy commitment offers little protection,” said Pio Smith, UNFPA Regional Director for Asia and the Pacific.
“Governments must turn those commitments into services young people can access, afford and trust. Investing in their health protects their choices, their education and their futures,” he added.
The report finds that most countries recognize adolescents in national health policies and have standards for services tailored to their needs. However, contradictory laws, insufficient financing and uneven implementation undermine these commitments.
It outlines 7 priorities for reform, including making adolescent sexual and reproductive health central to national health coverage plans, securing sustainable financing and improving the quality and reach of services.
Other priorities include reviewing discriminatory restrictions, clarifying consent rules, strengthening health information and community support, and involving adolescents in decisions about their care.
UNFPA has urged governments, development partners and civil society to translate the recommendations into funded action, with particular attention to adolescents who are out of school, displaced, living in poverty or otherwise excluded from services.
The report says universal health coverage will remain an unfinished promise until adolescents can access the care they need.

item.title: BB governor: P2P Bangla QR payments to launch in November
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank will introduce person-to-person transactions through Bangla QR in November, allowing people including rickshaw pullers and cobblers to send and receive money using their own QR codes, said Bangladesh Bank governor Md Mostaqur Rahman on Saturday.
He made the announcement at an event marking the launch of Bangla QR payments at United International University (UIU) in Dhaka, in partnership with ONE Bank PLC.
The initiative aims to expand digital payments among young people and make financial services more accessible, supporting the central bank's goal of building an inclusive and increasingly cashless economy.
The governor also said Bangla QR was being implemented in four phases.
The first involved introducing regulatory directives, making Bangla QR mandatory from July 1, while the second focused on testing the system's capacity to handle large volumes of transactions across interconnected payment service providers.
The third phase, launched on October 1, focuses on promoting wider adoption.
Charges for interoperable transactions between participating institutions have also been waived, regardless of the transaction amount, he said.
The fourth phase, scheduled to begin in November, will enable individuals to transfer money directly to one another using Bangla QR codes.
Mostaqur said the system's average daily transaction volume increased from Tk37 crore in the first week of June to around Tk180 crore in the last week of September, representing more than a fourfold rise.
However, he said the progress was only an initial step, adding that daily transactions of around Tk3,000 crore would indicate that the system had reached a more meaningful level of adoption.
He also highlighted the government's digital public infrastructure initiative, which aims to integrate digital identity, digital payments and data exchange to simplify access to banking and other public services.
ONE Bank managing director Muhit Rahman said the introduction of interoperable transactions had significantly increased activity through the bank's mobile financial services.
Monthly transaction volumes, previously around Tk2 crore, rose to Tk15-20 crore following the introduction of inter-institutional transactions from July 1, he said.
Rahman said transactions of up to Tk2,000 through Bangla QR would be free for customers and merchants under the applicable arrangement.
ONE Bank, however, would provide the service free of charge to UIU students, he added.
He said wider adoption of digital payments could bring people outside the formal financial system into banking services. Transaction records could also help financial institutions better understand customers' financial behaviour and potentially facilitate future lending and investment services.
Rahman added that the growing use of digital payments could transform traditional branch-based banking over the next three to five years.
As part of the initiative, UIU has been working to establish a cashless campus, bringing teachers and students under the service over the past two weeks, with plans to expand participation further.
UIU Vice-Chancellor Md Abul Kashem Mia said the university was introducing dynamic Bangla QR codes for individual students, allowing them to pay tuition fees and other charges more conveniently and reducing the risk of payment errors.
Students will also be able to share their QR codes with family members, enabling them to make payments through banks. QR-based payments have also been introduced at campus food courts, allowing students to pay their bills digitally.
The event featured demonstrations at participating business stalls, giving students and guests the opportunity to experience Bangla QR payments firsthand.
BB governor Mostaqur also held an interactive session with students on digital payments, financial innovation and the future of banking.
ONE Bank and UIU said the partnership aims to increase awareness and adoption of digital payments among young people while contributing to a more inclusive and interconnected financial ecosystem.

item.title: Portugal suspend Cristiano Ronaldo after national team walkout
item.description:
Cristiano Ronaldo has been provisionally suspended as the Portuguese football federation announced Saturday it had opened disciplinary proceedings against the 41-year-old following his decision to walk out on the national team.
Ronaldo apologised to supporters earlier this week while criticising Portugal coach Jorge Jesus and said he would serve any "suspension that is imposed" on him.

item.title: They’re not lying
item.description:
If a person’s story changes in the weeks following an alleged sexual assault, are they not telling the truth?
It’s a criticism I’ve seen on social media and heard in the public conversation surrounding the lawsuit filed in September 2026 by a plaintiff known as Jane Doe, a former student at Cornell University, accusing seven male students of rape.
Initially, Doe discussed events with a friend but reportedly didn’t identify them as assault. It wasn’t until weeks later, when her experience was labeled as a gang rape by others, that she came forward to authorities.
Survivors are often questioned about how they relay their stories. When societal expectations about how rape survivors should respond do not align with the victim’s experience, it’s easy to assume that the victim is lying and the assailant is innocent.
Research indicates 60% to 70% of female rape survivors do not identify their experience as rape. That’s especially true for college students.
Instead, rape survivors often describe their experience in more general terms, referring to it as “bad sex” or “miscommunication.”
That’s both because of how sexual assault affects a survivor’s mind, brain, and body and because of how society thinks about rape.
In my experience as a psychologist doing crisis intervention work with rape and sexual assault victims, it is very common for survivors to prefer to continue as if the assault never happened and to be driven by a strong desire to return to normalcy.
While this seems counterintuitive, understanding the biological and psychological survival processes that sexual assault can activate may help explain why this response is perfectly logical.
Trauma’s immediate impact
Immediately following a rape, survivors -- whether they characterize their experience as rape or not -- often experience myriad symptoms broadly referred to as rape trauma syndrome.
These symptoms include self-blame, emotional dysregulation, and feelings of fear and humiliation. These symptoms often lead to problems with sleep, headaches, muscle tension, and fatigue.
Psychologists generally diagnose symptoms consistent with rape trauma syndrome as acute stress disorder. Acute stress disorder reflects the unique psychological reactions immediately following trauma, whereas the longer-term effects are characterized as post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD.
People with acute stress disorder experience at least nine symptoms across several categories, including avoidance of trauma reminders, persistent negative mood, and dissociation -- defined as a disconnection between thoughts, feelings, and bodily sensations.
Other symptoms include intrusive experiences like nightmares or flashbacks, feeling like they are re-experiencing the trauma, constantly being on high alert, and having overly intense emotional reactions to reminders of the traumatic event.
The brain on trauma
During acute stress, the brain shifts into survival mode.
Two of the main bodily systems activated during this period are the limbic system and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. The limbic system controls emotions, memory, and behaviour. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis controls how the body responds to stress by regulating hormones like cortisol.
These systems mobilize the body’s key survival responses -- fight, flight, freeze, and fawn.
When the limbic system and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis kick in following trauma, the internal commotion that ensues takes over the brain’s ability to control thinking, planning, and decision-making.
This effectively prevents the brain from making accurate sense of what happened and from coping with the trauma in a healthy way.
Self-blame and denial are protective
For rape survivors, a common outcome of this neurobiological storm is self-blame -- a tendency to hold themselves responsible for the events that led to the trauma.
Generally, people believe they live in a world that feels safe and predictable, and they tend to adhere to the just world hypothesis, which posits that good things happen to good people.
To preserve the illusion of control, safety, and predictability, survivors blame themselves in an effort to restore order to a world that has been incredibly shaken by trauma.
Rape survivors often experience hindsight bias -- the belief that they should have been able to predict or prevent an assault.
This belief, which further reinforces self-blame, is fortified by a culture in which rape prevention programs tend to focus on women as opposed to men, leading women to believe they alone are responsible for and can prevent rape.
Then there’s denial, a defense mechanism that can take the form of avoidance of or dissociation from the trauma.
Because the reality of what has happened is overwhelming to the brain and psyche, denying or ignoring it provides a defense from the flood of emotion that follows trauma and helps reestablish a sense of stability.
Common rape stereotypes -- for example, that rape is mainly committed by strangers in a novel situation, not by acquaintances during everyday experiences -- reinforce these feelings. In fact, statistics indicate that 80% to 90% of women are raped by someone they know.
Judging a changing story
A person assessing the reactions of a rape and trauma survivor generally does so in a calm and collected frame of mind. Yet the actions they are judging were made under extreme duress.
For a survivor of rape, an inability to clearly name the assault for what it was is a common outcome of the biological and psychological factors at play during acute stress.
This denial functions to preserve their identity and sanity during acute stress, restore order to their world and help them make rational sense of what has happened to them.
Breaking through these self-preservation mechanisms often takes time -- time that observers too often misinterpret as a false accounting of what actually happened.
Michele Patterson Ford is Senior Lecturer in Psychology, Dickinson College. This article previously appeared in The Conversation and is being reprinted under a Creative Commons-Attribution/No Derivatives license.

item.title: Carrying the world upon your shoulders
item.description:
“I’m alright. I’m okay.”
We say it with such ease. Sometimes we mean it, sometimes it is simply the answer we have learned to give while carrying worry, fatigue, or loneliness we cannot quite put into words.
Behind a casual “I’m fine” may be someone trying hard to hold everything together, someone who needs to be heard but fears being judged.
When our body hurts, we seek treatment. But when our mind struggles, too many of us remain silent.
In Bangladesh, this resounding silence meets a deficiency of care. The 2018-19 National Mental Health Survey found that 18.7% of adults and 12.6% of children aged 7-17 experienced mental health conditions.
Reported treatment gaps exceeded 92% for adults and 94% for children. Behind these figures are people and families navigating distress with little professional help.
Resources remain painfully limited. A WHO-supported report published in 2025 noted that mental health received just 0.44% of Bangladesh’s total health budget in 2021 , with two-thirds of that spending directed towards mental health hospitals. Care closer to home needs far greater investment.
We need services that people can reach, afford, and trust. Our experience points to three priorities.
Bangladesh’s mental health policies must translate into accessible services:
This cannot be a singular effort. The government, private sector, and civil society all have to act in concert.
And each of us can begin with a small act of kindness: Ask how someone is doing, then make time for the answer.
We owe people a world where “I’m struggling” can be spoken without shame and met with compassion, dignity, and care.
Zahida Fizza Kabir is a social entrepreneur and CEO at SAJIDA Foundation.

item.title: Year later, Gaza ceasefire promises mostly unfulfilled
item.description:
One year after US President Donald Trump declared the war in Gaza to be over, few of the long-term promises of the ceasefire have come to fruition.
Here is a list of some of the key points of the October 10, 2025 ceasefire and where things stand:
Three days after the agreement was announced, Hamas freed the 20 remaining living hostages seized during the group’s October 7, 2023 resistance campaign.
The captives’ return was a key priority for Israel, whose public had agonized over their fate.
The ceasefire anniversary also marks one year of quiet for Israel from the Gaza front, with no rocket attacks by Hamas.
The group’s missile inventory was depleted by near-constant Israeli bombardment, which damaged or destroyed the vast majority of buildings in the Palestinian territory.
The US military set up a command post with foreign allies near the Gaza border to monitor the truce.
Israel has reduced its level of attacks but has kept striking Gaza on a near-daily basis.
Israeli strikes have killed some 1,450 Palestinians since the ceasefire, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which operates under Hamas and whose figures are considered accurate by the United Nations.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is in a tight election race, has vowed to kill everyone involved in the October 7 resistance campaign.
Netanyahu said on the attack’s anniversary that 4,000 out of 6,000 “Hamas monsters” had been killed.
Israeli forces were allowed to stay in 53% of Gaza under the terms of the ceasefire, but a year later they control about 70% of it, according to official accounts.
The second phase of the agreement was supposed to include a political transition away from Hamas, and technocrat Ali Shaath was appointed head of a new National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).
Hamas announced in July that it was disbanding its governing body and handing over Gaza’s administration to the US-blessed NCAG.
But Hamas effectively remains in charge of security in Gaza, and Shaath has taken a low profile.
The Palestinian Islamist movement elected a new leader, Khalil al-Hayya, in July. Shortly afterwards, the group announced it would give up its weapons, a step hailed by Trump as a breakthrough.
But Israel has been sceptical, with Netanyahu demanding verifiable decommissioning of all weapons down to individual guns.
Hamas has not gone ahead with disarmament, and Israel has refused to reciprocate by starting to withdraw forces.
Trump set up a new global body for the deal dubbed the “Board of Peace,” tapping as key figures former British prime minister Tony Blair and Bulgarian diplomat Nickolay Mladenov, who serves as “Gaza high representative.”
Trump, a critic of foreign aid, in January promised $10 billion in US funding to the board he controls, and Gulf allies have pledged more, but no money is known to have made its way to Gaza reconstruction.
In September, the board proposed a $2.45 billion Gaza recovery plan at a meeting of its members and stakeholders, in an effort meant to span over six months.

item.title: Russian strikes kill 11 including 3 children
item.description:
Russian strikes on Ukraine’s southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia on Saturday killed at least 11 people, including three children, according to regional authorities.
Ukrainian national police said Russia had targeted residential neighborhoods in the city with “five guided aerial bombs” early Saturday morning, hitting two residential buildings.
The strikes came a day after Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami in a renewed diplomatic push to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“The toll from the air strikes on Zaporizhzhia continues to rise. At present, 11 civilians have been killed. Among them are three children,” said Mykhailo Semikin, head of Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration.
He said rescuers were continuing their search for people under the rubble.
An AFP correspondent at the scene saw people being pulled from the rubble by Ukrainian emergency services.
“We saw people under the rubble -- a woman, her husband and a child,” one volunteer rescuer, Daniil Pishkin, told AFP.
He added that he saw two people rescued from the wreckage but “unfortunately there was a little girl who died.”
A resident of one of the buildings that was hit, who identified herself as Iryna, 69, said she just had time to seek refuge in the toilets after receiving an air raid warning.
She said her two neighbors were killed.
“They were 75 years old. They were simply thrown out there, onto the street. They didn’t make it to the hospital,” she told AFP.
The Zaporizhzhia region, located just a few dozen kilometers from the front line, and its capital by the same name have been the target of frequent strikes.
Russia has intensified its strikes on Ukrainian territory in recent months, causing a growing number of civilian casualties.
Diplomatic efforts mediated by the United States to end the war more than four years since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have so far yielded no results.

item.title: Yemen govt forces say advancing against Houthis around key waterway
item.description:
Yemeni military sources told AFP on Saturday their forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait but have not yet secured control of the waterway, after the government launched an operation to capture lost territory.
The Saudi-backed government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the pro-Iran group seized Yemen’s entire western coastline in a lightning offensive.
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandab area but they claimed to have repelled the assault.
“Saudi-led forces attempted to advance from the Ras al-Ara area in Lahj governorate towards the area south of Bab al-Mandab,” Hizam al-Asad, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, told AFP.
“However, our forces repelled them outside the Bab al-Mandab zone, inflicting heavy losses in personnel and equipment and forcing the survivors to retreat.
“Our forces maintain control over Bab al-Mandab, Mayun Island, and the remaining areas along the country’s western coast,” he said.
Sources from the military of Yemen’s internationally recognized government also said Mayun Island -- located in the heart of the strait -- remained in Houthi hands as fighting continued.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.
Clashes in western Yemen, specifically around the strait, had killed at least 63 people in the past 24 hours, military sources from both sides told AFP on Saturday.
Thirty-five members of government forces had been killed, while 28 Houthis had died, the sources said.
On Friday a Yemeni military source confirmed to AFP that their forces had launched a “major operation” in the strait region, supported by air power from Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s government.
After four years of relative calm, Yemen’s civil war reignited in July before the Houthi gains on Yemen’s western coastline.
Saudi Arabia leads an international military coalition helping the Yemeni government fight the Houthis.
Early on Saturday the coalition said it had destroyed more than 130 Houthi targets in a “large-scale operation.”
The Houthis’ Al-Masirah TV channel reported on Saturday that enemy strikes had targeted the Bab al-Mandab area.
It also reported four Saudi strikes on the capital Sanaa’s international airport on Saturday, a day after saying two were killed in a Saudi strike on the airport.
In addition to battling Yemeni government forces on the ground, the Houthis have also been firing on targets inside Saudi Arabia, attacking transport hubs, oil facilities and other civilian sites with drones and missiles.
Riyadh said Friday that attacks on the Saudi capital’s international airport had killed three people the previous day.
Saudi Arabia has been retaliating with strikes on key Houthi targets inside Yemen. Houthi media reported on Friday that two people had died in attacks on the airport in the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa.
Ordinary civilians have been paying the price for the renewed fighting in one of the world’s poorest countries, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.

item.title: Turkiye social media ban for under-15s takes effect Nov 1
item.description:
Turkiye on Saturday formally declared a ban on the use of social media for under-15s, scheduled to come into effect on November 1.
It has joined a growing number of countries legislating to protect children and teenagers from the harmful effects of online platforms.
The official state journal published the decision following the adoption of a law by parliament in April.
It stipulates that social media providers must “take the necessary technical and administrative measures, including age verification, to implement” protections for young people.
“No service likely to produce an addictive effect in children may be offered.”
Countries including Australia have introduced restrictions on social media for children and others such as Britain and France are pushing to do the same.
They aim to protect children from digital risks such as screen addiction, lack of sleep, bullying and eating disorders.
Rights groups have complained of restrictions on freedom of expression in Turkiye targeting LGBTQ communities, the media and the political opposition. Numerous social media accounts have been blocked in recent weeks.

item.title: Rizvi: Khaleda Zia, Tarique Rahman laid groundwork for July uprising
item.description:
BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi Ahmed has said former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman laid the groundwork for the July uprising of 2024.
He made the remarks at a memorial meeting organized by the Shaheed Jehad Smriti Parishad at the National Press Club in Dhaka on Saturday, marking the 36th death anniversary of Nazir Uddin Jehad, a student leader killed during the anti-autocracy movement in 1990.
Speaking as the chief guest, Rizvi said Jehad had traveled from Sirajganj to participate in the movement against then military ruler HM Ershad and sacrificed his life for the cause.
He said Jehad’s sacrifice, alongside 9 years of sustained protests and resistance, contributed to the fall of Ershad’s autocratic regime and helped strengthen the movement for the restoration of democracy.
“The July uprising of 2024 did not emerge in a single day,” Rizvi said, adding that it was the culmination of a prolonged struggle against what he described as authoritarian rule.
Rizvi said Khaleda Zia had maintained her uncompromising stance despite facing what he alleged were false cases, physical torture and imprisonment over the years. Tarique Rahman, meanwhile, continued to lead the movement from abroad, he added.
According to Rizvi, the struggles led by the 2 BNP leaders helped create the conditions that ultimately led to the July uprising.
Criticizing the previous government, Rizvi alleged that the forces defeated in the 1990 anti-autocracy movement and those ousted in 2024 were linked by a common political legacy.
He accused the previous government of presiding over widespread corruption, the looting of public resources, the depletion of bank funds and the laundering of thousands of crores of taka abroad during its 17-year rule. He also alleged that enforced disappearances and killings had been used to suppress political opposition.
Rizvi claimed that supporters of the previous regime remained embedded at different levels of the administration and society.
He urged the government to identify corrupt officials and those allegedly involved in abuses under the previous administration and take strict action against them.
“There should be no leniency towards those who carried out crossfire killings, killed people and plundered public money,” he said, adding that the public would support the government if it took firm action against wrongdoing.
Turning to the upcoming Durga Puja celebrations, Rizvi said Bangladesh had a long tradition of communal harmony, with people of different faiths participating in one another’s religious festivals.
However, he expressed concern that forces opposed to the current political order might attempt to create unrest around the festival.
He called on BNP leaders and activists, as well as members of the public, to remain vigilant and help protect Puja mandaps to ensure that members of the Hindu community could celebrate the festival peacefully and without fear.
The meeting was chaired by BNP Standing Committee member Amanullah Aman, president of the Shaheed Jehad Smriti Parishad. Former Dhaka University Central Students’ Union general secretary Khairul Kabir Khokon and former assistant general secretary Nazim Uddin Alam jointly moderated the event.
Among those who addressed the meeting were 1990 Students’ Struggle Council president Md Mustafizur Rahman Babul, BNP Chairperson’s Advisory Council member Habibur Rahman Habib, former Begum Rokeya Hall vice-president and MP Shirin Sultana, former Dhaka College vice-president and BNP volunteer affairs secretary Mir Sarafat Ali Sapu, and former Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal general secretary Saif Mahmud Jewel.

item.title: Mahdi Amin: Govt plans support for students failing SSC exams
item.description:
Prime Minister's Adviser for Education and Primary and Mass Education Mahdi Amin on Saturday said the government is formulating a permanent action plan to support students who fail to achieve expected results or are unsuccessful in the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) examinations. Under the directive of the prime minister, the plan will include technical training, language education, seed funding for small businesses and if necessary, an opportunity to retake failed subjects within three months, he said.
Mahdi Amin made the remarks while addressing the "Challenged Students Convention 2026" as the chief guest at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre in Agargaon.
Campaign for Popular Education (CAMPE) and Plan International Bangladesh jointly organized the convention, chaired by CAMPE Executive Director Rasheda K Chowdhury.
Mahdi Amin said around 0.69 million students had failed to achieve their expected results in this year's SSC examinations, stressing that academic performance should not determine their future.
He said students interested in technical and vocational education would be connected with local Technical Training Centres (TTCs), while those with promising business or innovative ideas could receive seed funding to start small businesses.
Short-term language courses lasting three to six months in Japanese, Korean, Chinese and European languages would also be introduced to help skilled workers explore international employment opportunities, he added.
Regarding the proposal to allow students to retake failed subjects within three months instead of waiting a year, Mahdi Amin said the government was considering it positively and hoped that changes would be introduced soon.
He said poor examination results could stem from various factors, including financial hardship, teacher shortages, inadequate classrooms and family problems. The government was working to address these challenges, he added.
"Life cannot be judged on the basis of certificates. Performing poorly in one subject does not diminish anyone's talent or creativity," he said.

item.title: The physics, economics, and market reality of curved monitors
item.description:
For 70 years, the display industry had one engineering religion: flatness.
When LCD panels took over from cathode ‑ ray tubes in the early 2000s, they quietly ended the era of curved screens—a shape dictated not by design, but by the physics of vacuum ‑ tube displays.
The industry declared victory. The perfectly flat screen became the baseline, then the standard, then the commodity.
Then, roughly a decade ago, the industry decided to curve the screens again.
This change is not about following trends or marketing strategies. It is an acknowledgment that for seven decades, the display was optimized for itself rather than for the person in front of it.
The ASUS ROG Swift OLED PG39WCDM, a 39-inch 800R curved OLED ultrawide, is the most aggressive commercial example of this contradiction today. (I owe thanks to Global Brand PLC, the authorized ASUS distributor in Bangladesh for providing this review unit, though the analysis remains strictly independent.)
Now, here is how this contradiction plays out in real life: imagine spending eight hours staring at a big, flat screen. Your eyes are not stationary.
They are constantly moving across the screen, from the code editor to the browser, from the data dashboard to the chat window. Each sweep asks your neck to turn.
Occupational health research consistently documents that if you look sideways beyond 35 degrees from the center, your neck muscles experience measurable strain over time.
The screen does not cause you pain right away. It just accumulates the debt silently.
The 800R curve exists to cancel that debt. Everything that follows is an honest accounting of whether it works, and what it costs to try.
Why the industry finally bent
The “R” in 800R stands for radius, measured in millimeters. The math works inversely: the smaller the number, the tighter the curve.
The 1800R gives a gentle curve, while 1000R is often described as “matching the human visual field”— a marketing term that is approximately, but not precisely, true.
The distinction between 1000R and 800R is categorical.
At 1000R, the curve feels natural for your eyes. It stops penalizing you for sitting close to a wide screen, but that is about it. At 800R, the design actively assists you.
When you sit exactly 80 centimeters from the panel, every pixel, from the dead center to the far corners, is at the exact same optical distance from your eyes.
The edges stop behaving as periphery. They become present. Your eyes stop wandering and start focusing.
The panel stops feeling like a wide wall you have to move around to see everything, and it starts acting like a concave cockpit: every window, tool, and file is within natural visual reach without you having to turn.
That is the whole reason the 800R design is the most effective.
So, where is the catch?
The selfish display
The 800R curve is the most focused single-user piece of display technology the consumer market has ever produced.
By optimizing every pixel for one viewer at the dead center of the curve, it actively degrades the experience for anyone else.
A colleague standing next to you sees distorted geometry: the far edge appears pinched, and straight lines bend.
This is precisely why curved televisions failed commercially in living rooms a decade ago. The engineering is structurally hostile to shared viewing.
The limit is absolute. If your workday involves frequent side-by-side collaboration, this monitor answers the wrong question entirely, regardless of its other credentials. Stop here.
But for the single-user command center focused on tasks like coding, data analysis, video editing, or gaming, this structural challenge becomes a benefit.
The design that might bother a second viewer is the same design that helps the first person concentrate. The display acts as a boundary that worth something real.
The limitation is not a flaw.
The hidden tax
The PG39WCDM's packaging is the first honest signal of what you are getting. The box is enormous, but the display inside is not.
Once the 800R arc wraps those 39 inches around your peripheral vision, the horizontal footprint is comparable to a standard 34-inch flat panel. The curvature makes it feel compact.
The depth is not.
A tightly curved display needs strong structural stability.
The stand of the display takes up more than 30 centimeters of desk depth.
On a standard 120-centimeter desk, that pushes the keyboard to the edge and takes away the little extra space most people use unconsciously.
The obvious solution is a VESA monitor arm. But the 800R curvature makes this more expensive than it appears.
The panel's center of gravity is closer to the mount than a regular arm accounts for.
A heavy-duty arm that can handle the weight costs approximately BDT 8,000 additionally.
You have to include it in your total cost of ownership calculation.
The text clarity problem
The display uses a 3440x1440 WOLED panel covering 39 diagonal inches.
The pixel density lands at approximately 96 PPI, below the 110 PPI threshold that Windows has historically treated as the baseline for comfortable text rendering.
The WOLED subpixel structure compounds the concern, as the panel uses a red, white, blue, and green layout.
Windows ClearType rendering assumes standard RGB.
Sub-100 PPI plus non-standard subpixels is a formula for visible fringing: the kind that makes fine text in spreadsheets and code editors uncomfortable to read for long periods.
However, in practice, at 80 centimeters, with ASUS’s Clear Pixel Edge algorithm running, the fringing is not noticeable under normal use.
But you can spot it if you move close to the panel and consciously look for it.
The WOLED trade-off is real, but it is almost completely invisible at the viewing distance the display was engineered for. The fear is understandable, but the actual practice is not the issue.
The color performance closes a gap that mattered more two years ago.
The display offers factory calibration, VESA-certified True Black levels, and 99% DCI-P3 coverage, along with a 240Hz refresh rate and 0.03ms instantaneous response time.
Color-critical studio work still belongs on a specialized ProArt display. Everything adjacent to it belongs here.
The Economics
The Tk230,000 price tag demands a real economic justification, not just a list of features. It needs a comparison.
The honest alternative is not a cheaper curved monitor.
It is a dual-panel configuration: two high-quality 27-inch 1440p IPS monitors at Tk60,000 each, a dual-monitor arm at Tk10,000, and remaining Tk100,000 for storage, peripherals, a sound system, or a laptop upgrade.
That is a setup a serious user would genuinely consider at the same budget.
The case for the PG39WCDM against that alternative rests on three specific claims.
First, a single-panel workspace eliminates the dead zone between two monitors where windows get lost and the cursor breaks continuity.
Second, no IPS panel, no matter the cost, matches an OLED substrate for True Black, response time, or maintaining color accuracy for long periods, which is critical for anyone doing creative and productivity work from the same desk.
Third, OLED panel costs are dropping faster than IPS premiums are rising. Buying before the price compresses is the wrong framing; buying at the leading edge of mass adoption has historically been the smart move.
The market backs up that third claim.
TrendForce Q2 2026 data shows that ASUS is leading the global OLED monitor market with a 23.1% share.
Market Intelo estimates the global curved monitor market at $5.8 billion in 2025, projecting growth to $9.6 billion by 2034 at a 6.8% CAGR.
Asia-Pacific commands 38.5% of that revenue and is the fastest-growing region. Bangladesh is definitely part of that growth, not just watching from the sidelines.
ASUS is not a brand making a bet on curved OLED. They are the brand that emerged victorious in the first round of a market that is still in its infancy.
Verdict
The debate between curved and flat is framed as a battle where one technology must eventually defeat the other. That framing is wrong, and it produces the wrong verdict.
The correct question is: what problem are you actually trying to solve?
Flat displays solve a universal problem well: a stable, shared, glare-manageable display surface for the widest range of users and configurations.
Curved displays, on the other hand, solve a specific problem better.
That problem belongs to a specific user, at a specific focal distance, in a specific working posture, doing a specific category of work.
The PG39WCDM is a machine built for one person, doing focused solo work, at 80 centimeters, for eight or more hours a day.
Every engineering decision on this panel, from the 800R arc and OLED substrate to the 240Hz refresh rate and factory calibration, is optimized for that exact configuration.
Deviate from it, and you pay a measurable cost. Stay inside it, and you get the best single-panel productivity and performance display currently available at a reasonable price.
If you are a solo operator, the curve is not just a visual preference; it is a structural decision about how you work.
And for everyone else, the flat screen is still the right answer. Not a compromise. An honest answer to a different question.
The writer is a contributor and tech enthusiast
